title: Violin Sonata in A major
hook: A wedding present in which one gentle tune keeps returning, each time in a new guise.

painting.title: Listening to Schumann
painting.collection: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels
painting.pairingNote: Painted in Brussels three years before the sonata was first played in public there, it shows a woman lost in music, her face hidden in her hand.

facts: Franck wrote the sonata in 1886, at 63, as a wedding present for the Belgian violinist Eugène Ysaÿe, who was 28. On the morning of the wedding, 26 September 1886 in Arlon, a friend handed it over; after a hurried rehearsal, Ysaÿe and the pianist Marie-Léontine Bordes-Pène played it to the guests.

The first public performance followed on 16 December in Brussels. According to Vincent d’Indy, a pupil of Franck who was there, the daylight faded during the concert and no lamps were allowed in the gallery, so the two players performed the last three movements from memory, almost in the dark.

The sonata is a famous example of [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]]: the violin’s first gentle tune comes back, transformed, in every movement, and other themes travel between movements too. The finale is a [[canon|canon]], one instrument following the other with the same melody.

Franck first thought of the opening movement as slow. Ysaÿe preferred it a little quicker, and Franck marked it Allegretto. The piano part is unusually hard, with wide stretches written by a composer who had very large hands.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dreamy song (I), a storm (II), a free improvisation (III), a sunny canon (IV).

movements.heading: Allegretto ben moderato
movements.summary: A quiet, swaying song. The piano opens with a few soft, unsettled chords, and the violin enters with the gentle rocking tune that is the seed of the whole sonata. The piano has a broader, more passionate tune of its own, which the violin never plays.

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s tune
mainIdeas.description: calm and rocking, rising a little and falling back, in a lilting rhythm of three-beat groups.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s tune
mainIdeas.description: louder and fuller, a song for the piano alone.

stops.hear: A few soft piano chords, rocking gently, that do not settle
The violin enters with a quiet, swaying tune
stops.happening: The main theme, the seed of the whole sonata

stops.hear: The violin stops; the piano alone plays a broad, warm, louder tune
stops.happening: The second theme, which belongs to the piano

stops.hear: The violin returns with its swaying tune
The piano’s tune returns, bigger than before, and the music swells

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Both instruments quieten; the violin’s tune fades on long, soft notes
stops.happening: A gentle close in A major

notice: Hum the violin’s first tune when it enters. You will meet it again, changed, in all three later movements.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A storm in D minor. The piano rushes in with dark, swirling figures, and the violin answers with an urgent, leaping tune. In the middle the music almost stops, and the dreamy world of the first movement returns for a moment, before the storm breaks again and finally clears into D major.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: fast, rolling figures in the piano, low and loud.

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s cry
mainIdeas.description: a passionate tune that leaps upwards.

mainIdeas.name: The calm
mainIdeas.description: a slower, singing theme for the violin over rippling piano notes.

stops.hear: The piano alone, fast and stormy, rumbling up from the bass
The violin enters with an urgent, leaping tune
Calmer: the violin sings a slower, gentler melody over rippling piano notes
The storm returns; short pieces of both themes are thrown between the instruments
Everything slows down almost to a stop; quiet and dreamy
stops.happening: A slow interlude. A shape from the first movement drifts back

stops.hear: The stormy music builds up again
The music brightens and speeds up

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Strong, bright closing chords

notice: Listen to the slow interlude near ≈ 3:45. For a moment the storm forgets itself and remembers the first movement.

movements.heading: Recitativo-Fantasia. Ben moderato – Molto lento
movements.summary: The most free and mysterious movement. The piano softly recalls the opening tune; the violin answers alone, in phrases like speech, as in a [[recitative|recitative]]. Then a new, warm melody arrives, grows to a powerful climax and sinks back, and the movement ends in darkness.

mainIdeas.name: The recitative
mainIdeas.description: the violin alone, free in rhythm, like someone thinking aloud.

mainIdeas.name: The new melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, warm tune for the violin over rippling notes in the piano. It will come back in the finale.

stops.hear: Slow, soft piano chords; a memory of the first movement’s tune
The violin answers alone, in free, speaking phrases
Piano and violin take turns: the piano offers, the violin replies
A new, warm melody in the violin over flowing piano notes
stops.happening: The melody that will return in the finale

stops.hear: Both instruments grow louder and louder
The music calms and slows

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Soft, dark chords
stops.happening: The movement ends in F-sharp minor

notice: Remember the warm melody at ≈ 2:40. Franck brings it back twice in the finale.

movements.heading: Allegretto poco mosso
movements.summary: Sunlight after the dark. The piano begins a simple, warm tune, and a moment later the violin plays exactly the same tune, one bar behind, as in a round. This [[canon|canon]] keeps returning, and between its returns the melody from the third movement comes back, once quietly and once at full power.

mainIdeas.name: The canon tune
mainIdeas.description: simple and singing, in A major, shared between the two instruments one bar apart.

mainIdeas.name: The returning melody
mainIdeas.description: the warm tune from the third movement.

stops.hear: The piano starts a warm, simple tune; a moment later the violin follows with the same tune
The two lines rise and chase each other
A familiar melody returns, calm and singing
stops.happening: The melody from the third movement

stops.hear: The canon tune again, in a new key
stops.happening: The tune returns, as in a [[rondo|rondo]]

stops.hear: Darker and more restless; fragments pass between the instruments and the tension grows
A loud climax: the third movement’s melody, now at full strength
The canon tune once more, back home in A major

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Bright, ringing closing chords
stops.happening: A joyful end in A major

notice: In the canon, try to follow only the violin. It is always one step behind the piano, never catching up.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Itzhak Perlman was 23 and Vladimir Ashkenazy 31 when they recorded the sonata in London in October 1968.

threads.title: One tune, many lives
threads.body: The violin’s first tune returns in the second movement’s interlude, opens the third, and stands behind the finale. That is [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]].

threads.title: Two equals
threads.body: The piano is never just an accompanist. It opens the first two movements on its own, owns a theme in the first and leads the canon in the last.

threads.title: From dark to light
threads.body: The keys tell the story: A major, a D-minor storm, a dark F-sharp-minor ending, then the sunlight of A major again.
